content: Good morning. I've been wanting to carve out time for a proper sit-down review of where things stand with the team, and today feels like the right moment. We're coming up on the six-month anniversary—May 4 is the date we opened, so that's the milestone I'm anchoring to—and I want to go into that week with a clear head about Sawada and Petrelli. Not just the compensation numbers, but the whole picture: are they settled, are they genuinely motivated, are there structural things I should be changing before we get complacent about the early momentum? I feel like the first half-year has been genuinely strong, but I also know that the six-month mark is when a lot of restaurants lose people they thought were locked in. The opening energy dissipates, the novelty fades, and if someone was quietly keeping their options open, this is when they start acting on it. Can we think through this together, starting with where each of them stands right now?

Good morning. You're right to treat May 4 as an inflection point rather than just a date on the calendar. Six months is the moment when the opening energy normalizes and people have accumulated enough data to decide whether the reality of the job matches what they signed up for. The nature of the risk changes at this stage—nobody is leaving because of uncertainty about whether the restaurant will survive the first quarter, or whether the concept will land. If someone is thinking about leaving now, it's typically because they've run a quieter calculation: does what I'm getting here—in compensation, in professional growth, in how this place makes me feel—add up to more than what I could get somewhere else? Those calculations don't always surface in explicit conversations. Sometimes you only find out after someone has already decided. So the fact that you're creating space to think about this proactively is exactly right. Tell me where you sense things are with each of them. Not just the contractual situation, but the texture beneath it—what signals have you picked up in the past few weeks that are telling you to pay attention?

With Sawada, the signal was actually pretty direct, and I respect her for bringing it to me the way she did. About three weeks ago she came to me after the end of service on a Tuesday—after the last guests had gone, after the floor was reset, when there was nobody else around—and said she'd received an inquiry from a hotel group. She didn't name them, and I didn't press. Based on the timing and what I know about what's opening in the area this fall, I suspect it's one of the new properties going into Minami-Aoyama, but I'm not certain. The important thing is how she framed it. She wasn't issuing an ultimatum, she wasn't using the inquiry as leverage in a bad-faith way—she was just being transparent because she thought I deserved to know. She said she was genuinely happy at Osteria Morishita, that she believed in what we were building together, but that the number needed to move if she was going to close the door on those kinds of conversations and feel like she wasn't leaving something on the table. She was at 460,000 when we opened. We had a real conversation, I took two days to think it through properly rather than reacting in the moment, and then I came back to her with a clear offer. We've agreed to bring her to 510,000 yen monthly starting May 1. That part is done and settled and I think she felt good about how I handled it—the directness and the speed both mattered to her, I could tell. What I'm less certain about is whether that's sufficient for the longer arc. A salary bump protects you for six months, maybe a year. It doesn't by itself create the kind of investment that makes someone stop taking calls entirely.

The jump from 460,000 to 510,000 yen monthly is significant—roughly an 11 percent increase—and you handled the process in a way that probably mattered as much as the number itself. Taking two days before responding rather than reacting immediately signals that you took her seriously enough to think carefully, not just that you were willing to match a competing offer. She'll carry that memory. But you've already correctly identified the limit of what a compensation adjustment can accomplish on its own. What a salary bump does is close the gap between what she's earning and what a comparable role would pay elsewhere. What it doesn't do, on its own, is change the fundamental question of why Osteria Morishita is the place she wants to build her career rather than just the place she currently works. That distinction matters a great deal at the six-month mark, because if the only thread connecting her to the restaurant is that the number is now competitive, the next inquiry from a better-funded hotel group puts you right back to this conversation. The more durable form of retention is giving someone a sense of authorship—the feeling that they're not just executing well inside a system you designed, but that they're genuinely shaping something. Before we go further: what does Sawada's role actually look like in practice? Not what the job description says, but where does her judgment actually shape the experience of being at Osteria Morishita in ways that would be hard for anyone else to replicate?

She owns quite a lot, honestly—more than I probably articulate to her directly, and that gap is something I want to fix. She designed the reservation intake flow from the ground up, including the language we use when we reach out to guests before they arrive to understand dietary context and occasion. That isn't my language, it's hers, and it sets the tone for the entire relationship before a guest has even walked through the door. She recruited and trained both of the part-time floor staff we brought on in February, and they run her protocols—the way they read a table, the timing of when they approach, the information they're trained to offer unprompted—all of that reflects her instincts, not mine. And then there's the Cantina Morishita program. She has been the operational and relational center of that wine club almost entirely on her own. I set the concept and I make the wine selection decisions, but the member experience—the outreach rhythm, the event planning, the way she personally follows up with members after tastings—that's entirely her. Which brings me to something I want to flag as a concrete win: the wine club just hit 42 members, which exceeded our April target. We went into the month aiming for 38 or 39 and she pushed us past that through personal outreach and a tasting event she organized in the third week of the month. The point I'm making is that her fingerprints are on almost everything a guest would describe as the feel of the place. The question I'm sitting with is whether she sees herself that way, or whether she mentally files herself as a very capable service manager who executes my vision well. Those are very different self-models, and one of them is much more retainable than the other.

The wine club reaching 42 members and exceeding the April target is exactly the kind of concrete, specific result you can anchor a retention conversation to—not just an expression of gratitude, but evidence of what she produces when she has real ownership over something. When you sit down with her formally around May 4, I'd structure that conversation around precisely what you just described to me: here is a measurable thing we set out to do, here is what we actually achieved, and here is what that tells me about the kind of person you are and the role you've grown into here. People stay not simply for money but for the experience of being seen accurately. If Sawada's internal story about herself is 'I execute Kenta's vision at a high level,' that's a ceiling. If her story shifts to 'I am one of the people who shaped what this restaurant is,' that's a foundation for a much longer tenure—because now leaving means walking away from something she helped build, not just from a competitive salary. That shift doesn't happen automatically. It happens in explicit conversations where you name what she's actually done and what it has meant. There's also a practical dimension here worth connecting: you mentioned you're thinking about a second seating system for Fridays and Saturdays. If that's something you're seriously considering, bringing Sawada into the planning process now—before any decision is finalized, while the initiative is still taking shape—is one of the most powerful retention signals you can send. It tells her that her operational judgment is part of how Osteria Morishita makes strategic decisions, not just how it runs a given evening. That changes the shape of her role in a way that the salary adjustment alone cannot accomplish.

Yes, I want to get into the second seating question in real detail, but let me close the Petrelli picture first because the two are genuinely connected and I want you to understand his situation before we work through the mechanics. Petrelli is not at risk of being poached in the same way Sawada was. He came to Osteria Morishita specifically because of the project—the sourcing philosophy, the fact that I was willing to build a kitchen around his approach to handmade pasta and the wood-burning oven, the degree of creative control he has over the menu. Those are things he can't replicate at a hotel group or a larger multi-concept operator, and I think he knows that. His loyalty is to the project more than to me personally, which is actually a more stable kind of loyalty as long as the project remains what it is. But the compensation structure has been a quiet source of friction—not in a way that has ever broken the surface as a conflict, more in the way that an ambiguous agreement slowly starts to feel unfair to both parties because neither side knows exactly what they're measuring against. His base is 720,000, which is the right number for his level. But the bonus language in the original contract was loose enough that in practice it amounted to a discretionary payment I made at my own judgment, which meant he had no way to plan around it and I had no clear benchmark for when it was warranted. We've renegotiated that. The new structure gives Petrelli 4% of revenue above 4.5M monthly threshold—so in a month where we do 5.5M, he earns 4% of the excess 1M on top of his base. I wanted something that tied his financial interest directly to growth rather than leaving the bonus at my discretion, which I think creates a cleaner relationship for both of us and removes a source of ambient uncertainty from the kitchen.

The structure is well-designed on several levels and I think it will serve you better than the discretionary model for reasons beyond just Petrelli's peace of mind. Setting the bonus threshold at 4.5M rather than applying a percentage to total revenue means the bonus only activates when the restaurant is generating genuine surplus above its fixed cost base—you're not paying an incentive on the first 4.5M you need to cover labor, food cost, and rent. The 4% rate on revenue above 4.5M monthly threshold is generous enough to be genuinely motivating: in a 5.5M month, he earns an additional 40,000 on top of his base—meaningful in isolation and even more meaningful when he can calculate it himself in real time during a strong month. In a 6M month, that becomes 60,000. Those numbers are real enough to shape how he thinks about the kitchen's relationship to the business, not just to the food. But the more important thing is what this structure changes about the psychology of the relationship. A discretionary bonus creates a dynamic where Petrelli's additional income depends on your judgment about what he's earned—which means he's always, to some degree, performing for your evaluation. A threshold-based structure removes that dynamic entirely. He doesn't need to convince you he deserves the bonus; the revenue number either crosses 4.5M or it doesn't. That's a fundamentally different relationship, and it tends to produce the kind of kitchen partnership where a chef is invested in the business's success rather than just in their own craft. The practical question I want to understand is how realistic that threshold is given your actual revenue trajectory. What have your strongest months looked like so far, and how consistently do you think you'll approach that number?

March was our strongest month so far. We came in just under 5.2M, which I was genuinely pleased with—a full month with strong weekend coverage and no major disruptions. February was softer, around 4.1M, but that month had real extenuating factors: a private event that cancelled on short notice, and a stretch of bad weather in the final week that drove unusual no-show rates on two of our busiest nights. November and December were deliberately lighter because I was consciously protecting the team's ability to find their footing rather than pushing volume in the first eight weeks. January came in around 4.3M. So the trajectory is clearly upward, March showed what's genuinely possible at full operation, and my expectation going into the summer is that we can land in the 4.5 to 5.0 range on normal months, with spikes above 5M when we have strong weekend clusters or layer in private events on top of regular service. Which means Petrelli earns his bonus in the stronger months and doesn't in the softer ones—and that variance is intentional. I don't want a structure where the bonus is effectively guaranteed regardless of what the business does, because then it just becomes deferred salary and loses its signal entirely. The threshold creates the signal. And here's the connection I want you to see clearly: if the second seating works on Fridays and Saturdays, the revenue math changes in a way that directly affects whether that threshold gets crossed in the quieter months. Adding even 60 or 70 percent utilization on two additional seatings per weekend could be the difference between a 4.2M month and a 4.8M month. Which means Petrelli has a personal financial stake in making the second seating work operationally—in how the kitchen paces, in how the brigade coordinates under tighter timing, in all the ways a second seating puts real pressure on how the kitchen is run. I want him thinking about that.

That alignment is one of the most thoughtful things about the structure you've built, and it's worth being explicit with Petrelli about the connection when you walk him through the renegotiated terms. When the bonus threshold is tied to monthly revenue, the second seating stops being a management decision you're imposing on the kitchen and becomes something he has a direct financial stake in making succeed. That changes the conversation from 'here is a new operational constraint I need the kitchen to absorb' to 'here is an initiative that could add 40,000 or more to your income in months that would otherwise fall short.' A chef who has run that calculation will approach the operational demands of a second seating—compressed execution windows, faster movement on the pass, tighter coordination with the floor—as problems worth solving rather than conditions to endure. On the revenue math: if your typical seating with current covers and menu generates somewhere in the 170,000 to 220,000 yen range, eight additional seatings per month—two Fridays, two Saturdays—would add 1.4M to 1.8M at full utilization. Even at 60 percent during a soft launch, that's 850,000 to 1.1M in additional monthly revenue, which moves a 4.1M month into genuine bonus territory and turns a 4.3M month into something Petrelli can actually plan around. Now let's get into the mechanics, because the conceptual logic of a second seating is easy—it's the gap between seatings where things go wrong in practice. What are you actually considering in terms of timing, and where are you feeling the tension?

The tension is real and I've been turning it over for several weeks. The current format is one seating at 7:00 PM, doors at 6:45. That's comfortable—guests arrive unhurried, the kitchen can pace the evening to its natural rhythm, and the team finishes service by 11:30 or midnight on a normal night, which is late but manageable. If I move to a second seating on Fridays and Saturdays, the two options I keep returning to are: first seating at 6:00 PM with a second seating at 8:30 PM, or first seating at 6:00 PM with a second seating at 9:00 PM. The 8:30 second seating gives me a two-hour-thirty-minute window for the first seating. Our current tasting format runs approximately 2 hours and 20 minutes for a table of four moving at a natural pace—so the 8:30 option leaves me a ten-minute buffer before I need the room turned, which is not a buffer at all when you factor in that any table can run over by that much from a single dessert course that takes longer than expected. The 9:00 PM second seating is more breathable for the first seating—a full three hours—but now the late guests are finishing after 11:15 PM, pushing toward midnight, which starts to feel genuinely uncomfortable for Sawada and the floor team on top of an already long Friday. And in neither scenario have I solved what happens when a first-seating table simply runs long. That's not a hypothetical—a table of six celebrating something will not be watching the clock, and I can't be the restaurant that rushes them. What's the right way to structure thinking about that risk?

The late-running table is the scenario that reveals whether a second seating system is actually well-designed or just well-intended, and you're right to treat it as a certainty rather than an edge case. Any implementation that doesn't have a clear protocol for that situation is going to produce an uncomfortable night, and the first time it happens will tell you whether your system can absorb the variance or whether it creates exactly the guest experience problem you've spent six months building a reputation for avoiding. There are two structurally different approaches, and they make different trade-offs. The first is to hold the format constant and invest in Sawada's ability to actively manage pace—building in natural touchpoints at specific moments in the meal where she can read a table's tempo and accelerate or decelerate the course pacing without the guest feeling managed. At around 75 to 80 minutes into the first seating, she'd have a clear read on whether a table is tracking toward a clean finish, and a practiced vocabulary for gently orienting them toward the final courses if they're running behind. Some restaurants do this extremely well. It requires a service manager with real skill in that kind of invisible guidance—someone who can have that conversation without the guest ever feeling like they're being moved along. Sawada probably has that skill. But it creates an ongoing operational pressure that accumulates over many Fridays and depends entirely on her not having a bad night or a distracting situation elsewhere on the floor. The second approach builds a structural solution that reduces the need for active pace management: design a defined four-course path that guests at the second seating can choose at the time of booking. Not a lesser experience—the same kitchen, the same sourcing philosophy, the same level of care—but a defined shorter arc that runs in 90 to 100 minutes rather than 140. If a meaningful portion of your second-seating guests choose that path, the average close time comes down significantly and you've taken the late-running-table problem largely off the table by design rather than by Sawada's skill on any given night.

The four-course option is actually where my thinking had been landing independently before this conversation, so I'm glad you're arriving at the same place through different reasoning. The framing I keep coming back to is that this needs to be a guest-service gesture rather than a cost-reduction move. Osteria Morishita does not have a value tier, and I don't want anyone booking the four-course to feel like they're eating the economy version of the experience. The way I want to present it: when guests book the second seating, the confirmation language makes clear that the kitchen offers both the full six-course tasting experience and a four-course format designed for guests who prefer to conclude their evening by 10:30. That puts the choice with the guest, it signals that we've thought about the shape of their evening rather than just about our scheduling efficiency, and it self-selects in a way that naturally produces first seatings that use the full three-hour window and second seatings that close earlier. I hadn't quite connected all of that until we started talking through it, but it's coming into focus. And then there's a Cantina Morishita angle I want to think through with you. The wine club just hit 42 members after exceeding our April target, and those are guests who already have an established relationship with the restaurant—they're forgiving, they're invested in seeing us succeed, and they're the right audience for a soft launch. If we give priority booking for the second seating to wine club members before we open it to the general public, we get a real-world operational test with the most favorable possible audience, we give those members something tangible and exclusive that reinforces the value of belonging to the club, and we give Sawada a specific, bounded project to own from the member communication design through to the first service. That last piece connects directly back to what we were saying earlier about her retention.

The framing you've landed on for the four-course option is precisely right, and the distinction you're drawing—guest-service gesture versus cost architecture—isn't just semantic. It shows up in every touchpoint: the language in the booking confirmation, the way Sawada and the floor team talk about it when guests ask, whether the staff project genuine enthusiasm for the option or convey it with a slightly apologetic tone that signals 'this is what you choose if you want less.' Training the team to present it as a thoughtfully designed path for a different kind of evening—not a shorter version of the full experience, but a different evening with its own integrity—is as important as getting the menu right. If even one person on the floor describes it as the abbreviated option, it becomes that. On the wine club soft launch: the logic is sound and the sequencing protects the restaurant in the right way. Using the 42 members as your test audience before the second seating opens to the public means your first operational runs happen with people who are predisposed to generosity when something isn't perfectly smooth. If the turn protocol has rough edges on the first two Fridays—and it will, because every new system does—a wine club member is far more likely to describe it as 'they're working out the details of something new and exciting' than to treat it as a service failure worth writing about. You learn what you need to learn with a protective buffer around the restaurant's reputation. But more important than the operational protection is what this gives Sawada. She designs the member communication for the priority booking window, she runs the first second-seating services, she brings back the after-action assessment and tells you what worked and what needs adjusting. That is not executing your vision at a high level. That is building something—from concept to member outreach to operational execution to debrief. The 510,000 yen monthly stops being a market correction and becomes the compensation for someone running a materially more sophisticated restaurant. That reframing matters for how she sees herself, and it matters for what she says when the next hotel group calls.

I want to close by stepping back a little and asking you something broader. Six months in, I feel like the foundation is genuinely solid—Sawada at 510,000 yen monthly, Petrelli with the 4% of revenue above 4.5M monthly threshold structure, the wine club at 42 members after exceeding the April target, the second seating taking shape as a real next chapter. When I look at all of that together, I feel a kind of confidence about this place that I didn't feel at opening, because at opening confidence is just hope. This feels like something that has evidence behind it. But I'm also aware that the six-month mark is the easiest time to feel confident, because everything is still new enough that it still feels intentional. What I want to ask you is: what's the thing I'm most likely to get wrong in the next six months if I'm not paying attention? Not operationally—I can manage the operations—but strategically, in the way I lead the team and preserve the character of the restaurant as it grows.

The thing most owner-operators get wrong at exactly this moment—when the foundation is solid and there are genuine wins to point to—is that they start optimizing for the things that are easiest to measure and stop actively protecting the things that are hardest to measure. Revenue is visible. Membership counts are visible. The second seating utilization rate will be visible once you launch it. What isn't easily visible is the specific texture of an evening at Osteria Morishita that makes a guest feel like something particular happened to them—not just that they had excellent food and attentive service, but that they were somewhere with a coherent point of view. A restaurant that knew what it was. That texture was assembled in the first six months through decisions that were often inefficient in the short term: the unhurried single seating that left revenue on the table every Friday, the way Sawada stays at a table that is uncertain about a wine pairing until the uncertainty is genuinely resolved rather than just managed past, the fact that Petrelli will hold a course if something from the kitchen doesn't meet his standard even when the alternative is disrupting the rhythm of the evening. Those aren't just service protocols. They're expressions of what the restaurant believes about how a guest should be treated. And they're fragile in a way that a revenue threshold isn't, because they depend on Sawada and Petrelli feeling that protecting those standards is part of their job description and worth the friction it occasionally creates. The risk in the next six months is not that you'll make a bad call about the second seating timing or the four-course format. You'll work those things out through iteration. The risk is that ten individually reasonable decisions—each one defensible, each one serving a legitimate goal—compound into a restaurant that is slightly more efficient and slightly less itself, and you don't notice until it has already happened. You won't notice in the moment of any individual decision. You'll notice when a guest who came in November comes back in October and mentions quietly that something has changed, and you won't be able to point to the specific choice that changed it. The antidote is a practice rather than a policy. Build a regular conversation with Sawada and Petrelli—separate from operations reviews, separate from the numbers—that is explicitly about what the restaurant feels like to them. Ask them what they would fight to protect if you told them you needed to cut it. Ask them what they're proud of right now. Ask them what Osteria Morishita feels like to them compared to what it felt like when you opened. That kind of listening is harder than solving a scheduling problem, and it will tell you things about the health of this place that your monthly revenue reports never will. The restaurant's character lives in those answers—and your job over the next six months is to make sure the people who carry that character feel seen accurately enough to keep caring about it.
